Rapid KL to replace Kelana Jaya Line track in stages from this Sunday

KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 9): Rapid KL will carry out track replacement work on the Kelana Jaya Line Light Rail Transit (LRT) in stages covering seven phases, starting Sept 13 until September 2027. Rapid KL in a statement Wednesday announced that this improvement work is being carried out to ensure that the track infrastructure is always at a high level of safety and reliability. According to the statement, stations involved in the track replacement work will begin operating at 9.30am compared to the usual 6am, while stations not involved will operate as usual according to schedule. The track replacement work involves Gombak and Taman Melati stations on Sept 13, 20 and 27, followed by the second phase for Universiti, Kerinchi and Abdullah Hukum stations (Nov 15, 22 and 29), as well as the third phase covering Dato’ Keramat, Jelatek and Setiawangsa stations (Jan 10, 17 and 24, 2027). "The fourth phase involves Universiti, Kerinchi and Abdullah Hukum stations on 14, 21 and 28 March 2027, followed by the fifth phase involving Masjid Jamek, Dang Wangi, Kampung Baru, KLCC and Ampang Park stations on 9, 16 and 23 May 2027," the statement said. Meanwhile, the sixth phase involves Taman Jaya, Universiti, Kerinchi and Abdullah Hukum stations on 11, 18 and 25 July 2027, while the final phase involves Gombak and Taman Melati stations on 12, 19 and 26 Sept 2027. Ticket machines at each station involved will be temporarily closed until 9.30am and users can obtain tickets at the station counters while Rapid KL and Touch 'n Go product users can continue their journey as usual. "Rapid KL will also provide a free shuttle bus service connecting the stations involved during the track replacement works," the statement said. To facilitate passenger movement, station staff, auxiliary police and 'Prasarana Troopers' volunteers will be stationed at the affected locations, while signboards and information leaflets will also be provided. Kelana Jaya Line users are advised to check the track replacement work schedule and alternative bus movements via the website www.myrapid.com.my and Rapid KL's official social media channels. "This track replacement work is important to ensure that the Kelana Jaya Line infrastructure continues to be at a high level of safety and reliability to support more reliable rail services in the future. "Rapid KL appreciates the cooperation and support of passengers throughout the implementation of these infrastructure improvement works," the statement said. Uploaded by Liza Shireen Koshy
Not just skin deep? What happens when beauty moves into the health aisle

Ingestible beauty supplements include drinks that promise to support healthier skin, hair and nails from within. Photo: 123rf Looking good is no longer just about what you apply to your skin. It is about what you put into your body – or so it seems. There is a fast-growing trend towards ingestible beauty products, from supplements to drinks that promise to support everything from a glowing complexion to healthier hair and nails from within. It certainly challenges the old adage that “beauty is only skin deep”. Yet questions remain about how effective these formulations and their active ingredients really are. Safety is another issue that warrants closer examination, particularly as more beauty products move from the ­bathroom shelf to the kitchen cabinet. Dr Lim Ing Kien, a practising medical doctor, points out that these products are already subject to regulation. He estimates that about 80% of beauty ingestibles on the Malaysian market are classified as food supplements. According to Dr Lim, these typically come in formats such as liquids, sachet powders and, increasingly, gummies. They fall under the Food Act 1983 and Food Regulations 1985, overseen by the Health Ministry’s food safety and quality division. The remainder, he says, are sold as conventional health supplements. These are available in capsule or tablet form and require registration with the National Pharmaceutical Regulatory Agency, including a MAL registration number. The distinction is partly down to the format. Capsules and tablets can resemble medicines, potentially making it easier for consumers to mistake supplements for pharmaceutical products. Cosmetics and topical skincare products, meanwhile, fall under a separate regulatory framework, Dr Lim explains. Unlike medicines and health supplements, cosmetics are generally notification-based rather than subject to full registration, with comparatively limited testing requirements. Cosmetic companies in Malaysia must notify the National Pharmaceutical Regulatory Agency (NPRA) before marketing their products, unlike medicines and health supplements, which require separate registration. When contacted by StarLifestyle , the Health Ministry confirms this in a press statement but still cautions consumers to remain vigilant. The issue is whether this is enough to address concerns about ingestible beauty products occupying something of a grey area. This is particularly pertinent as consumers may also assume that regulatory oversight means the products have been proven to deliver the promised results. Read more: What are multitasking cosmetics and why are they now a go-to beauty choice? Looking good goes beyond the surface As it is, beauty ingestibles are indeed having a moment. A report by market research and consulting firm InsightAce Analytic estimates that the global market was valued at US$4.2bil (approximately RM16.95bil) in 2024 and is projected to reach US$13.1bil (RM52.86bil) by 2034. International celebrities including Kourtney Kardashian and Elle MacPherson have also launched their own brands, selling wellness products designed to be eaten or drunk for their purported beauty benefits. In Malaysia, former television personality Marion Caunter offers “botanical beverages” under her own haircare brand, described as being “formulated with multivitamins” to enhance overall hair quality, thickness and lustre. Dr Lim says one of the turning points for the beauty industry was the Covid-19 pandemic. “People started thinking about prevention instead of correction, and they started thinking about health generally,” he says, noting that while beauty ingestibles were already on shelves before then, the category really took off in 2021. Pointing to skincare as an example, Lim says people often forget that the skin is an organ. “On the outside you have UV, pollution, heat. On the inside you have hormones, diet, stress, everything your body is doing. If you treat only the outside, you’re treating only half of it.” He adds that the idea of ­consuming products for beauty and wellness is hardly new in Asia. Drinkable collagen, he claims, can be traced to traditions ranging from Chinese herbal soups and Malay jamu to Indian Ayurveda. “Every one of those traditions has something you swallow or drink for skin, hair, general vitality,” he says. “Our grandmothers were doing this long before anyone called it a beauty trend. What’s new is the scientific evidence. We now have scientific data supporting the ingestible side.” He gives the example of studies like the treatment of melasma with ingested pine bark extract (Pycnogenol), and a placebo-controlled trial examining ingested fern extract (Polypodium leucotomos) as an add-on to sunscreen. Lim has also entered the market himself, launching his own range of “drinkable skincare” products. This raises an obvious question about potential conflicts of interest, particularly when the medical professional recommending a beauty ingestible is also involved in developing and selling it. Lim acknowledges that it may become a problem, but says he is transparent about his commercial interest, disclosing that he owns and formulated the product whenever he recommends it to patients. He argues that doctors can bring a valuable perspective to health-related businesses, given their understanding of patients’ needs and ability to assess scientific evidence. “What the patient actually wants matters more than what I recommend,” Lim says. “Some want a capsule, some want something to drink, some want neither, and any of those is a reasonable answer.” Broader convergence of health and beauty There is a broader expansion of what beauty means, with consumers looking beyond skincare and cosmetics to wellness practices that support both how they look and how they feel. Sleep therapy, stress management, nutrition, fitness and other aspects of holistic health are becoming intertwined with beauty. This shift is prompting healthcare companies to broaden their portfolios to include beauty and wellness solutions – and positioning themselves in an increasingly blurred market where looking good and feeling good are part of the same proposition. Sandy Tan, CEO of Optimax Holdings Bhd, says that consumers are becoming more proactive about their overall health and appearance, the reason being that people today are looking for sustainable ways to age well and maintain their quality of life. Optimax began as an eye specialist before expanding into aesthetics and holistic beauty services. Tan believes that research into healthy ageing and the connection between overall health and skin health has advanced significantly in recent years. Sandy Tan says consumers should not think that if a product is marketed for beauty, it must be effective or suitable for everyone. Photo: Optimax She however cautions that the growing popularity of these topics has also resulted in increased marketing, making it difficult for consumers to distinguish established science from emerging theories. “As a healthcare provider, we encourage consumers to evaluate claims carefully and look for credible clinical evidence rather than marketing promises,” Tan stresses. “While innovation is important, consumers should understand that scientific evidence develops over time, and not every trending ingredient or concept has been conclusively proven.” She adds that a person should not have to think that if a product is marketed for beauty, it must be effective or suitable for everyone. Her view is that professional advice is particularly important because supplements and wellness products may not work for some people. In the end, individual health conditions, medications and treatment goals should always be taken into consideration before incorporating them into a daily routine. At Neumax, Optimax’s aesthetics arm, medical doctor Datuk Dr Liow Tiong Sin serves as medical director, reflecting the increasingly medicalised nature of aesthetics. Tan says that beauty is, without a doubt, evolving from being largely appearance-focused to becoming part of a broader wellness journey. She observes that consumers are increasingly looking for solutions that support healthy ageing and long-term wellbeing rather than simply addressing visible concerns. “I believe this integrated approach will define the future of beauty, where looking good is increasingly seen as a reflection of overall health and wellbeing.” Read more: Refillable beauty is slowly gaining ground in Malaysia, here's why it matters Consumer awareness is always important At the end of the day, consumers have a responsibility to assess the claims made by brands. In February last year, the Health Ministry flagged a China-based cosmetics brand over suspected contraventions of the law in its marketing campaigns. While the products were intended for topical use, they were depicted in social media videos in ways that suggested they were edible. The case is a reminder that not everything seen online should be taken at face value – particularly when it comes to claims about beauty and health. Co-founder of local wellness brand Boony & Co, Boon Hau Hng, says that, in his experience, consumers are becoming savvier. He relates how his customers come in asking very specific questions about active ingredients. They take it seriously and want to know whether a particular product is safe for them or their family members to consume. “Everyone has been focusing on skincare for the longest time,” Boon says, referring to topical products. “But skincare is a great complement; it is not the be-all and end-all.” Boon Hau Hng (right) and Fam Swee Ying believe consumers are extremely savvy when it comes to health and beauty matters. Photo: The Star/Azlina Abdullah He admits that as the ingestible beauty market grows, marketing efforts by different brands are also getting louder, whereby consumers have to be extra careful to cut through the noise. On whether people let their guard down when it comes to beauty products compared with health products, Boon says what everyone expects is results. “Everyone is checking with AI first, but then they don’t even completely believe the answers they get,” he says. “Especially the younger generation. They will come in asking about the formulation of products. “So they don’t just believe everything they read or are told.” The other co-founder of the brand, his wife Fam Swee Ying, says ingestible beauty products also mirror some of the traits seen in the cosmetics market, including the fact that women continue to make up much of the customer base. This perhaps illustrates just how closely beauty and health have come together. She also points out that even skincare brands are seeing their customers become more discerning. “You will notice they are asking about specific active ingredients in a face cream,” Fam notes. “So it shows that consumers, buying beauty or other products no longer need you to hold their hands and tell them what to buy. They come in shopping for specific needs as well.” Ultimately, the growing overlap between beauty and wellness may mean that looking good is no longer simply about what happens in front of the mirror, but also about the choices we make beyond it. As the beauty shelf continues to expand into the wellness aisle, a little curiosity – and a healthy dose of scepticism – may be the best things consumers can bring to the shopping basket. Buying opportunity after sell-off at breweries?

This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on August 31, 2026 - September 6, 2026 THE country’s two listed breweries — Heineken Malaysia Bhd (KL: HEIM ) and Carlsberg Brewery Malaysia Bhd (KL: CARLSBG ) — saw a sell-off of their shares this month. It started after Heineken Malaysia announced lacklustre earnings for the June quarter, with net profit contracting year on year as subdued consumer sentiment weighed on revenue growth. Analysts slashed their earnings estimates, with several downgrading their calls on the stock. In a single trading day, Heineken Malaysia’s shares fell 10% from RM19.10 at the close on Aug 5 to RM17.10 on Aug 6. Carlsberg, which had yet to announce its quarterly earnings at the time, was also dragged down by jittery investors, falling 5.4% over the same period. Carlsberg closed at RM14.94 on Aug 6. The share price continued to decline for a week for Carlsberg and two weeks for Heineken before the slide eased. Carlsberg saw some rebound after the company announced its June quarterly earnings, which showed net profit and revenue increasing marginally. Analysts say the sell-off was partly justified given the big miss in top- and bottom-line performance, particularly in the case of Heineken Malaysia. Yet, others opine that the sell-off in Carlsberg was overdone. “The recent sell-off was partly justified by a genuine, sizeable miss in the top and bottom lines. The latest financial performance reflected subdued consumer demand and ongoing inventory normalisation across the customer and distributor network,” Fortress Capital Group CEO Datuk Thomas Yong tells The Edge. “But it does, to a certain extent, look like an overreaction — though not an unreasonable one given the lack of near-term visibility on when destocking ends, the consumer macro backdrop as well as the potential excise duty hike in the upcoming Budget 2027 [which is set to be tabled in parliament on Oct 9].” Given that the current price-earnings ratios (PERs) of both breweries are in the low teens, well below their historical median of close to 22 times, do they make a good buying opportunity? Malacca Securities head of research Loui Low opines that much of the near-term weakness has been priced in for the breweries following the sharp correction in their share prices. “At current valuations, the breweries look more attractive from a defensive and dividend-yield perspective, though excise duty and broader sin-sector policy risks may continue to cap valuations, especially around Budget 2027,” he says. Dividend yields, which have often been a lure for investors looking to invest in breweries, have certainly trended higher following the sell-off in their share prices. Carlsberg’s trailing 12-month (TTM) dividend yield now stands at 7.56% based on a share price of RM14.82, while Heineken Malaysia’s TTM dividend yield amounts to a whopping 9.43% based on its current share price of RM16.10. The breweries are generous with dividends, with Heineken Malaysia’s dividend payout at around 100%, while Carlsberg’s payout has ranged between 75% and 90% over the last five financial years. Following the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, the dividend per share for both breweries has increased. Fortress Capital’s Yong says the breweries are trading “cheap” compared with their own historical valuations and are also cheaper than their regional beverage peers. “Both operate in a two-player duopoly, with high regulatory barriers to entry. Hence, the current multiples look attractive on paper,” he notes, but also warns that the rise in excise duties is crimping consumer demand. Carlsberg managing director Stefano Clini mentioned in the press release for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026 (2QFY2026) that the brewer is seeing early signs of the 10% increase in excise duty affecting consumer demand and spending. During the tabling of Budget 2026 last year, the government had proposed raising excise duty on alcohol by 10% effective Nov 1, 2025. The hike, the first increase in nearly a decade, resulted in a new rate of RM192.50 per 100% volume per litre. The last time duties were raised was in 2016, when locally produced hard liquor duties rose by 150%, while beer and stout duties were rebased to RM175 per litre of alcohol. Policy risks are certainly an aspect investors are watching closely, especially with Budget 2027 just around the corner. The brewers have seen lacklustre earnings performance in recent times. Analysts say this is a normalisation effect post-Covid-19, when the reopening created a surge in demand and the subsequent restocking cycle has been unwinding. There is also anecdotal evidence that consumers, particularly younger people worldwide, are drinking more selectively and moderately. Meanwhile, Yong says structural issues such as cost-of-living pressures are squeezing discretionary spending, while the higher excise duty is widening the price gap with illicit alcohol. “All in all, near-term earnings weakness is mostly a normalisation/destocking story that should resolve, but the industry is sitting on top of a genuinely maturing, low-single-digit-volume-growth market where periodic tax shocks are now a recurring feature rather than a one-off event,” comments Yong. Malacca Securities’ Low concurs, noting that lower consumption among younger people could limit volume growth over the longer term, implying that future earnings growth will depend more on pricing, premiumisation and product mix. “While valuations have become more attractive, I think the upside may also remain capped for now. Without a stronger volume growth story, it may be difficult for the sector to command the higher valuation multiples seen previously,” he explains. Based on data obtained from parent company Carlsberg Group’s recent annual reports, the volume of beverages sold by the group in Malaysia and Singapore, measured in million hectolitres (hl), declined from 1.5 million hl in FY2023 to 1.33 million hl in FY2024 and further to 1.31 million hl in FY2025. The trend was in line with its Asia portfolio, where total beverage volume fell from 44.6 million hl in FY2024 to 43.5 million hl in FY2025. Malaysia and Singapore make up only 3% of the volume of its Asia market, while the bulk comes from China and Hong Kong, at 69%, as well as Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, at 28%. Beer accounts for 87% of total volume, while the remainder comes from its Beyond Beer category and soft drinks. As for Heineken Malaysia’s parent company, the group does not break down volume by country-specific markets. However, its data shows that volume in the Asia-Pacific region grew from 43 million hl in FY2023 to 45.3 million hl in FY2024 and edged up further to 45.5 million hl in FY2025. However, Heineken Malaysia’s revenue was flat at RM2.8 billion in FY2025 compared with FY2024, while net profit slipped to RM459.34 million from RM466.75 million. Interestingly, Carlsberg’s revenue slipped to RM2.26 billion in FY2025 from RM2.38 billion in FY2024, but net profit increased to RM377.2 million from RM340.7 million. Having said that, Carlsberg seems to be the preferred counter of the two. It has nine “buy” calls, with an average target price of RM21.49, implying 45% upside from its closing price of RM14.78 last Thursday. Analysts see Carlsberg as more resilient in terms of performance and have also pointed to its attractive dividend yield. “The overall consumption environment could get more challenging in 2H2026, but Carlsberg’s marketing and cost-optimisation initiatives should mitigate the impact. It now trades at an attractive valuation after the recent sell-off. We think this is overdone in view of its resilient performance and attractive dividend yield on offer,” says RHB Research in an Aug 17 report. For the cumulative six months ended June 30, Carlsberg reported net profit of RM181.86 million, up 3% from a year earlier, while revenue increased to RM1.22 billion from RM1.15 billion previously. The earnings were below analysts’ expectations, as they accounted for 47% of consensus forecasts, due to weaker-than-expected sales. As for Heineken Malaysia, analysts are split on the stock, with five “buy” and four “hold” calls. Three research houses downgraded their calls from “buy” to “hold” following its June-quarter earnings announcement. Heineken Malaysia’s 1HFY2026 net profit totalled RM154.98 million, 24% lower year on year, while revenue was also lower at RM1.09 billion, down 15.7% from a year ago. The results accounted for only 32% of analysts’ full-year forecast. CGS International Securities, which recently downgraded the stock, says while it trades at 16.1 times FY2027 PER and offers a 6.1% FY2027 dividend yield, it sees limited near-term rerating catalysts for the stock. It names potential excise-duty hikes in the Budget 2027 announcement as a downside risk, as these could exacerbate illicit activities. It also sees weaker consumer demand for alcohol and sluggish tourist arrivals weighing on revenue. The upside risks to its forecast include a stronger-than-expected recovery in consumer spending and on-trade demand, easing raw material and packaging costs, as well as higher-than-expected export volumes to Singapore. The average 12-month target price for Heineken Malaysia stands at RM21.61, giving it a 33.6% upside from its closing price of RM16.18 last Thursday. DPM Fadillah returns to Cabinet meeting after heart bypass surgery

KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 9): Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Fadillah Yusof on Wednesday returned to attend a Cabinet meeting after undergoing heart bypass surgery and taking medical leave to recuperate. In a Facebook post, Fadillah, however, said that on the advice of specialists at the National Heart Institute (IJN), he would remain on medical leave until Sept 27. “My deepest appreciation and thanks to Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim and all my Cabinet colleagues for their concern, prayers and support throughout my treatment. “I am very grateful and happy to be back with my Cabinet colleagues at today’s meeting,” he said. Fadillah, who is also energy transition and water transformation minister, said that during his medical leave, he would only attend Cabinet meetings in person. “May we all be blessed with good health and lasting well-being, and be able to carry out the responsibilities entrusted to us to the best of our ability,” he said. The Petra Jaya member of Parliament underwent heart bypass surgery at IJN on Aug 12, after being admitted to the institute on July 28. He underwent a coronary angiogram the following day. Singapore Airlines to seek tougher terms for any fresh Air India funding — Reuters

HONG KONG (Sept 9): Singapore Airlines, backed by state investor Temasek, is expected to seek greater influence over management and stronger governance rights before approving a capital injection into Air India, said two people familiar with the matter. The proposed conditions, which would be negotiated with Air India's majority owner Tata Sons, could include greater board voting power and requirements for the Indian carrier to narrow its losses, the people said. Temasek, Singapore Airlines' majority shareholder, would neither provide the capital itself nor intervene in the carrier's decisions concerning Air India, they added. The discussion of conditions comes after Reuters last month reported Air India was seeking about US$1.5 billion in fresh equity from its owners. Two other people said Tata had approved a US$1.1 billion infusion, representing its pro-rata share. Singapore Airlines holds the remaining 25.1% stake. All four of the people declined to be identified as the information is not yet public. In a statement, Singapore Airlines said its board would carefully evaluate any request for additional capital, taking into account Air India's business strategy, the group's operating cash flow and its other capital requirements. Temasek declined to comment on "speculation with respect to the points on Temasek." Tata and Air India did not respond to requests for comment. Limited influence The push for tougher terms reflects growing pressure on Singapore Airlines to justify increasing its investment in Air India, which posted a US$2.33 billion loss in the financial year ended March, weighing directly on the Singaporean carrier's profits. Singapore Airlines has lost money in several past overseas investments, and Tata said in July that Air India's turnaround could take up to a decade. The Indian carrier has appointed former Ethopian Airlines head Tewolde Gebremariam as its new CEO to replace former Singapore Airlines executive Campbell Wilson. Singapore Airlines has limited formal influence over Air India. Under a 2022 merger agreement that folded its 49%-owned Indian carrier Vistara into Air India, it received a single board seat, taken up by its CEO Goh Choon Phong. Its stake of more than 25% does, however, give it the power under Indian company law to block special resolutions covering major corporate matters, including mergers, share buybacks and voluntary winding up. Air India's funding request drew a call from an opposition lawmaker in Singapore for Temasek's funds not to be used to support the Indian airline. Singapore Airlines said on Tuesday that its investments in India have been and will continue to be funded by its internal resources, noting it had S$10.48 billion (US$8.29 billion) in cash reserves and S$3.24 billion in undrawn credit lines as of end-June. Temasek last month publicly backed Singapore Airlines' investment in the Indian carrier, saying it took a long-term view of the decision. Singapore's Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on Saturday that any decision to invest in Air India lay with Singapore Airlines, and that Temasek expected the airline to make investment decisions responsibly. The onus for setting safeguards, governance expectations and performance targets for any additional investment in Air India lies with Singapore Airlines, not Temasek, one of the people said. Singapore Airlines' strategy is to benefit from India's long-term aviation growth while managing the risks of a major airline turnaround, the person added, noting that Temasek backed similar bets on Indian companies in the past, including hospital operator Manipal Health. Temasek has built up significant exposure to India across sectors including healthcare, financial services, consumer and technology, and has cited the country as a key growth market in its portfolio. Policeman kills teacher wife at Thai school, kids safe
Highlight, South East Asia, Top World, World

The gunman returned home after the shooting in Chonburi province, southeast of Bangkok, where police were negotiating his surrender. (EPA Images pic)
BANGKOK: A police officer shot dead his teacher wife at the kindergarten where she worked in Thailand on Wednesday but all the children are safe, officials said.
The gunman returned home after the shooting in Chonburi province, southeast of Bangkok, where police were negotiating his surrender.
The incident is the latest shooting to rock Thailand, a month after a teenager shot his grandparents and then five staff and a pupil at his school, before killing himself.
Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region, and past promises of tightening gun laws have not prevented repeated shootings.
Sayan Klomaon, chairman of Nong Pla Lai sub-district council, told AFP the gunman - a policeman local to the area - came to the school at about 10:30 am (0330 GMT) and talked with his wife before shooting her.
No students saw the incident, as it happened outside the classroom, he said, adding that the gunman then left to go home, and since then all the children had been picked up.
In a statement on Facebook, Chonburi Governor Naris Niramaiwong confirmed that all 44 children were safely evacuated along with three teachers and three other staff members.
He said police had surrounded the house where the gunman was and were negotiating his surrender.
The motive remains unclear.
Naris ordered the kindergarten closed and said psychological support will be provided to children and staff who witnessed the incident.
In 2022, an ex-policeman armed with a gun and a knife stormed a nursery in northern Thailand and killed 24 children and 12 adults, in one of the country's deadliest massacres.

OpenAI says working with Samsung on next-generation chips, deepening cooperation

SEOUL (Sept 9): OpenAI is deepening cooperation with Samsung Electronics as the ChatGPT maker develops its own chips, expanding ties with the South Korean technology giant across semiconductors and enterprise AI services. "One of the areas where we have made the most progress and gained the most recognition with Samsung Electronics is our joint production and research on the next-generation chips we are developing," Harrison Kim, general manager of OpenAI Korea, said at a press conference in Seoul on Wednesday, without elaborating. Kim also said Samsung Electronics was "one of the largest-scale deployments of ChatGPT globally," saying the company's employees in Korea and overseas use ChatGPT for work across research and development, marketing and sales. Samsung Electronics said in a statement that it could not confirm information related to customers. In June, OpenAI unveiled its first custom artificial intelligence chip designed with Broadcom. OpenAI's ​engineers designed the chip, called Jalapeno, together with Broadcom for a task known as AI inference, the process of crunching data to answer queries in applications such as ​ChatGPT. OpenAI at that time said that Taiwan's TSMC would manufacture the chips. Last year, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix signed letters of intent to supply memory chips for OpenAI's Stargate data centre project. Kim said demand for memory chips would continue to grow as more advanced chips were needed to enable faster and more complex computing, making cooperation with South Korean semiconductor suppliers a priority for OpenAI's local office. The cooperation comes as Samsung broadens its use of generative AI. The company said in June that workers in its Device eXperience division, which oversees mobile phones, televisions and home appliances, would be allowed to use ChatGPT, Google's Gemini and Anthropic's Claude internally. OpenAI said the number of ChatGPT Enterprise users at South Korean companies and institutions had surged about 28-fold as of the end of August from a year earlier, as businesses broadened their use of artificial intelligence from individual tasks to company-wide operations. Companies were increasingly using AI across functions including legal, sales, finance, marketing and operations, OpenAI said. The company declined to provide absolute user numbers. South Korea had the largest number of paying ChatGPT subscribers outside the United States as of late last year, according to OpenAI. OpenAI expects adoption to accelerate following the Sept 4 launch of GPT-6 Astra, its latest model, which it said offered improved performance in computer use, professional work, science, coding and cybersecurity. Me and Time Harry Henry Julin Column , Opinion 09/09/2026 6:26 am Facebook X WhatsApp Telegram Email LET’S READ SUARA SARAWAK/ NEW SARAWAK TRIBUNE E-PAPER FOR FREE AS ​​EARLY AS 2 AM EVERY DAY. CLICK LINK I understand and appreciate time management and all that comes with it. Of course I do. I am a journalist, after all. I have been one since I was 20 years old. Deadlines are not strangers to me. In fact, they have been my constant companions for more than five decades. Journalists live by the clock. Newspapers do not wait. Editors do not wait. Readers certainly do not wait. News breaks when it wants to, not when it is convenient. Throughout my career, I have learned to respect time, chase time, measure time, save time, and occasionally curse time. Yet despite all that, I often find myself exhausted by it. Sometimes I feel suffocated by schedules, appointments, reminders, calendars, and alarms. There are moments when I wonder whether I have spent too much of my life managing time and not enough simply living in it. I am 73 now and still gainfully employed. Many people my age have retired, taken up gardening, or become professional supervisors of grandchildren. Not me. I am still working, still writing, still dealing with deadlines. But as I grow older, I find myself increasingly drawn backwards rather than forwards. My thoughts often wander to my childhood in a remote village in the Serian District. Perhaps that is normal. When one reaches a certain age, memory becomes less like a photo album and more like a favourite old film that keeps replaying itself. The strange thing is that the scenes I remember most vividly are not grand events. They are not achievements, celebrations, or milestones. What I remember most is freedom. Back then, time existed, of course, but it did not rule us. Other than school hours, we were largely free from strict timekeeping. Nobody carried a watch. There were no mobile phones, no digital calendars, no smart devices reminding us every few minutes that we were either late, early, or behind schedule. The sun was our clock. The crowing rooster was our alarm. The setting sun was our curfew. That was about it. As children, we roamed freely through the jungle trails. We fished in streams and wetlands near the paddy fields. We climbed trees whose names I can still remember, though sometimes I struggle to remember where I left my reading glasses five minutes ago. Life was wonderfully inconsistent. One day we might spend hours chasing fish. Another day, we would be hunting for wild fruits. On some days, we wandered around because wandering was an activity. No productivity targets. No strategic planning. No performance indicators. No one asked us to optimise our childhood. Looking back, I realise I was quite like Mark Twain’s Tom Sawyer. Not the whitewashed-fence entrepreneur part. I never managed to convince other boys to do my chores. But I certainly shared his appetite for adventure, mischief, and avoiding unnecessary work. Like Tom Sawyer, I regarded every river, path, tree, and hill as an invitation. The world was not something to be managed. It was something to be explored. Time stretched endlessly before us. A morning felt like a week. A school holiday felt like a lifetime. Waiting for Christmas or Gawai Dayak required a level of patience that would probably qualify today’s children for a psychological evaluation. Yet somehow, we survived. More importantly, we enjoyed ourselves. Then adulthood arrived. As adulthood often does, it came carrying clocks. At first, it was harmless enough. You start work. You learn punctuality. You learn responsibility. You learn that bosses become strangely emotional when employees arrive two hours late and explain they were observing the flight pattern of hornbills. Eventually, you adapt. I certainly did. City life has a way of disciplining people. In cities, time is not merely measured; it is weaponised. Everything has a schedule. Meetings start at a specific time. Buses leave at a specific time. Flights depart at a specific time. Bills must be paid at a specific time. Even leisure activities are scheduled. Some people actually schedule relaxation. Imagine that. One enters an appointment into a calendar: “4 p.m. to 5 p.m. — Relax.” The poor soul then spends the entire hour worrying about whether he is relaxing efficiently enough. Cities train us to become managers of minutes. The clock becomes a silent supervisor hanging over our lives. Tick. Tick. Tick. Not threatening. Just persistent. A gentle reminder that time is money. An even gentler reminder that somebody else usually gets the money. Over the years, I developed discipline. I had to. A journalist without discipline is merely a storyteller with overdue copy. I learned how to organise my work. I learned how to meet deadlines. I learned how to operate within systems. The skills served me well. They still do. Yet a small rebel survived inside me. A village boy hiding behind an ageing journalist. And that rebel developed a strategy. I call it stealing time. Not in any criminal sense, of course. No police officer has ever arrested me for possession of unregistered leisure. What I mean is that throughout my life, I have quietly stolen moments from the system. Small pockets of freedom. Fragments of unclaimed hours. Little islands of time that belonged entirely to me. A slow morning. An afternoon nap. A walk with no destination. A fishing trip. A day spent reading. An evening doing absolutely nothing useful. These moments may seem insignificant. To me, they are priceless. I suspect many people secretly do the same thing. They may not admit it openly. Modern society celebrates busyness. People wear exhaustion like a medal. Ask someone how they are doing, and the answer is often: “Very busy”. It is usually delivered with the pride of a soldier returning from battle. The implication is clear. Busy means important, successful, and productive. But I sometimes wonder whether we have confused activity with living. After all, a hamster on a wheel is extremely busy. Yet it never actually goes anywhere. Perhaps that is why I guard my weekends, public holidays, and annual leave so fiercely. Those periods become my little acts of resistance. When they arrive, I quietly declare independence. “Come what may,” I tell myself. The world can survive without me for a day or two. Remarkably, it usually does. The newspapers continue printing. The politicians continue talking. The economy continues wobbling along. Civilisation does not collapse because I choose to spend a morning drinking coffee and staring at the rain. This discovery was both comforting and mildly insulting. I had imagined myself indispensable. The world politely disagreed. So, I learned to embrace my temporary disappearances. Sometimes I travel. Sometimes I visit old places. Sometimes I sit. The older I get, the more I appreciate sitting. As a child, sitting still often felt like punishment. As an adult, it feels like a luxury. There is a certain joy in having nowhere to be. No urgent emails. No deadlines. No alarms. Just existence. When I find such moments, I often think about my village years. Not because life was perfect. It wasn’t. Village life had its hardships. People worked hard. Resources were limited. Comforts were fewer. But there was something valuable that modern life often struggles to provide. Space. Mental space. Emotional space. Time that felt owned rather than borrowed. Perhaps that is what I miss most. Not youth itself. Youth is overrated. Young people have energy but very little wisdom. Older people have wisdom but occasionally require assistance in locating their spectacles. Life insists on maintaining balance. What I miss is the feeling of unstructured time. The sensation that a day can unfold naturally rather than according to a timetable. The freedom to follow curiosity wherever it leads. Children possess this instinct naturally. Adults spend decades trying to recover it. The irony is rather amusing. As children, we want to grow up. As adults, we spend considerable effort trying to remember how it felt not to be adults. Perhaps that is one of life’s favourite jokes. The years teach us many things, but one lesson becomes clearer with age. Time is not merely something we manage. It is something we experience. Modern life encourages us to treat time like a resource. We save it, spend it, waste it, invest it, and budget it. But perhaps time is not a currency at all. Perhaps it is closer to a river. We do not own it. We travel through it. Some days the river moves quickly. Some days it moves slowly. Sometimes we fight the current. Sometimes we float. Either way, the river continues. At 73, I know I cannot return to those childhood days in Serian. The jungle trails have changed. The village has changed. The world has changed. Most of all, I have changed. Yet the boy who wandered through forests and wetlands still lives somewhere inside me. He emerges whenever I steal a little time from the demands of modern life, reminding me that not every moment needs a purpose, every hour needs to be productive, or every day measured by achievement. Sometimes, a day is valuable simply because it was lived. Perhaps that is the wisdom age slowly reveals. In youth, we believe we have endless time. In middle age, we try to control it. If fortunate, we eventually learn to make peace with it. The clock will keep ticking. The calendar will keep turning. The river will keep flowing. What matters is not how tightly we hold time, but how fully we inhabit the moments entrusted to us. So protect a little space for yourself. Watch the rain. Walk without purpose. Sit beneath a tree. Remember who you were before the clocks arrived. For life is not measured by deadlines met or appointments kept, but by those moments when time briefly ceased to matter — and we felt truly alive. ——————————————— ‘Life is what happens to you while you’re busy making other plans.’ — John Lennon (1940–1980), an English musician, singer, songwriter and peace activist, best known as a founding member of The Beatles, one of the most influential bands in music history. CLICK LINK ‘A great coach does not merely teach a player how to win; he builds the skills, character and confidence that allow the player to win without him.’ – A badminton fan This week, I feel particularly happy and proud of one Malaysian badminton coach who has been making waves overseas. His name is Wong Choong Hann, the former Malaysian international and former coaching director of the Badminton Association of Malaysia (BAM), who is now head coach of the Hong Kong badminton team. And what a job he appears to be doing. Two of his charges, Jason Gunawan and Lee Cheuk Yiu, reached the men’s singles final of the China Masters – an achievement that represents a significant milestone for Hong Kong badminton. For a Malaysian badminton fan like me, this is something worth celebrating. I follow badminton closely, and naturally I am all smiles whenever our Malaysian players perform well. Conversely, I can be rather sad and disappointed when our boys and girls fall well below expectations. But this time, I want to focus not on the players but on the coach. Following Hong Kong’s impressive showing, I came across suggestions that BAM should bring Choong Hann back into its fold. I beg to differ. Why should we always think that whenever a Malaysian coach does well overseas, we must bring him home? Perhaps we should look at it differently. Let me say this – let our Malaysian coaches shine overseas. Choong Hann has been in Hong Kong since 2023, after leaving his position with BAM. He took up the challenge because he wanted to step outside his comfort zone, and he has spoken positively about the experience of coaching outside Malaysia. That experience is valuable not only to him but also to Malaysian badminton. If a Malaysian coach can help raise the standard of badminton in another country, that is a reflection of the quality of our coaching system and the talent we have produced. Choong Hann is certainly not alone. Malaysia has produced a remarkable pool of coaches whose expertise is now sought after beyond our shores. Jeremy Gan has coached in Japan and is now part of Hong Kong’s coaching setup. Tan Bin Shen, formerly associated with Malaysia’s doubles programme, has also moved to Hong Kong. Then there is Lee Wan Wah, who has been involved with Japan’s national men’s team, and Tan Kim Her, who has made a name for himself in India. Chin Eei Hui has also taken her coaching expertise to New Zealand. These are not failures of our system. Quite the contrary. They are evidence that Malaysian coaching expertise has international value. For years, Malaysian badminton has benefited from foreign expertise. We have welcomed coaches from Indonesia, Denmark and elsewhere because we recognised that good ideas, knowledge and experience should never be restricted by nationality. Look at Indonesian coaches such as Hendrawan, who has made a significant contribution to Malaysian men’s singles, and Flandy Limpele, who served in Malaysia’s doubles programme. Then there was Indonesian legend Rexy Mainaky, an Olympic champion and one of the world’s most respected doubles figures, who joined BAM in a senior coaching role. BAM itself described his appointment as a move to strengthen and revitalise Malaysia’s doubles programme. We also had Denmark’s Morten Frost, one of the great names of world badminton, serving Malaysian badminton in senior technical roles. He brought a different perspective and different ideas to our system. So why should we hesitate when the reverse happens? If Malaysia can benefit from foreign coaches coming here, other countries should be equally entitled to benefit from Malaysian coaches going there. There is another important point which I must also stress. A coach who works overseas does not necessarily cease being an asset to Malaysia. He becomes an ambassador of Malaysian badminton. He carries with him our methods, experience, discipline and knowledge. At the same time, he learns from another badminton culture and another sporting system. That exchange can only be healthy. Imagine if more Malaysian coaches were given the opportunity to work in Japan, India, Hong Kong, China, Europe, Australia or elsewhere. They would return one day, if and when they choose to, with a much broader understanding of international badminton. And if they decide to remain abroad for a longer period, we should still wish them well. We should not regard every Malaysian who succeeds overseas as someone who must be brought home. Badminton is an international sport. Players, coaches, sports scientists, trainers and technical experts move across borders. Knowledge moves with them. Malaysia’s ambition should therefore not simply be to keep all our best people at home. It should be to become a country that produces so much talent that the world wants our players and coaches. That would be something to be proud of. Of course, BAM must continue developing a strong national coaching structure and ensure that Malaysian coaches who remain at home are properly rewarded and given opportunities to progress. There is little point in complaining about losing coaches overseas if we fail to make coaching an attractive and respected profession here. Indeed, a recent report noted that Malaysian coaches are in high demand abroad and highlighted the need for competitive remuneration to retain coaching talent. But let us not confuse retaining talent with restricting talent. If Wong Choong Hann is doing well in Hong Kong, let him continue doing so. If Jeremy Gan is contributing to Japanese or Hong Kong badminton, let him. If Tan Kim Her can help India produce better players, good for him. And if other Malaysian coaches receive offers from overseas, we should perhaps congratulate them rather than immediately asking: “When are you coming home?” Because sometimes the best way to serve Malaysian badminton is not necessarily to work in Malaysia. Sometimes, it is to go out into the world, prove what Malaysians can do, learn from others and leave a Malaysian footprint wherever we go. Let our coaches shine. Let our players shine. And when they do, let us be proud enough to say: They are Malaysians, and they are showing the world what Malaysians can do. —————————————– DISCLAIMER: The views expressed here are those of the columnist and do not necessarily represent the views of Sarawak Tribune. Appellate court quashes Guan Eng's RM50,000 defamation award from Zuraida, news portal

PUTRAJAYA (Sept 9): The Court of Appeal on Wednesday overturned a lower court's decision to order former local government minister Datuk Zuraida Kamaruddin and a news portal to pay RM50,000 to former finance minister Lim Guan Eng for defamation. A three-judge bench led by Datuk Mohd Firuz Jaffril, also dismissed Lim's cross appeal seeking an increase in damages. The case stems from an article published on news portal MalaysiaNow that quoted Zuraida regarding a housing project for former plantation staff in Bestari Jaya, Selangor. Zuraida's published comments were made during the Kuala Kubu Baharu by-election in 2024. The decision means Zuraida and MalaysiaNow need not pay any damages to Lim. The bench also ordered Lim to pay RM30,000 in costs to Zuraida and MNow Media Sdn Bhd, which operates the MalaysiaNow news portal. Mohd Firuz, who sat with Datuk Ahmad Kamal Md Shahid and Datuk Amarjeet Singh Serjit Singh, said three elements need to be proven in the defamation case: that impugned the article referred to Lim, that it was published and that it was defamatory. The bench found that while the first two elements were met, they disagreed the article was defamatory. “Based on the three pairs of eyes (on the bench), we find the words complained off by Lim did not give rise to be defamatory of Lim. We conclude so on the basis that Lim said he did not approve the low-cost housing project due to a lack of funds. “What gives rise to the complaint was that the housing and local government minister (Nga Kor Ming) said they now have the money and the project can go on. This has nothing to do with the allegation that Lim is unfit for office (as finance minister). The timing of the two issues differs,” Mohd Firuz said. The low-cost housing project was not approved in 2018, when Lim was finance minister. Zuraida was commenting on what Nga said in 2024 during the Kuala Kubu Baharu by-election. 'High Court erred' The appeals court bench felt the High Court judicial commissioner's handling of the suit was unsatisfactory. “The High Court's final analysis found that the defence of justification was not met based purely on lack of documentation (to show the rejection of the project) and not based on what transpired between them (Lim and Zuriada). “The second defence put by Zuraida that what she said was fair comment was not considered. Further the High Court judge found there is malice, and this negates the defence of fair comment and qualified privilege. There are inconsistent findings by the High Court judge as in one portion she found there was malice but in another she wrote there was ... no evidence of malice,” the judge said. Mohd Firuz said the High Court judge had erred in not considering the defence of the defendants. “It is on these broad reasons that there are obvious errors in the High Court judgment and the judgment cannot stand. We allow Zuraida's appeal and dismiss the cross-appeal (by Lim) on quantum,” he said. Shah Alam High Court judicial commissioner DR Shoba Rajah had ruled in February that MalaysiaNow’s article quoting Zuraida was defamatory, and ordered them to pay RM50,000 damages to Lim. Lim had cross-appealed on the RM50,000 damages awarded by Shoba Rajah. Lim had claimed that Zuraida’s comments published by MalaysiaNow meant he had not approved the funds for the construction of more than 200 units of low-cost housing. The former finance minister claimed this was untrue or otherwise slanderous and/or libellous, false, and disparaging of him. Zuraida and MNow Media's counsel Nizamuddin Abdul Hamid, who appeared with Mohd Adib Isa of Messrs Zharif Nizamuddin, had told the bench that the article was not defamatory and that the appeal should be allowed as on one hand, the judicial commissioner found there was malice but in another portion of her written judgment found there was no malice. The lawyer had also argued that the High Court was wrong to seek documentary proof of Lim’s rejection of the low-cost housing project, as former housing and local government director general, Datuk N Jayaselan, had testified to the rejection. EU to help cities tighten screws on Airbnb, holiday rentals

The Affordable Housing Act aimed to give cities legal cover, clarifying when authorities can act without falling foul of EU single market rules. (EPA Images pic)
BRUSSELS: European cities will gain more leeway to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb under plans to bring down housing costs in tourism hotspots that the European Union is to unveil Wednesday.
The European Commission is to lay out conditions under which local authorities can limit short lets, as part of an "affordable housing" package that seeks to address what EU chief Ursula von der Leyen has called a "social crisis".
"Nurses, teachers, and firemen cannot afford to live where they serve. Students drop out because they cannot pay the rent. Young people delay starting families," she said in a speech last year highlighting the issue as a priority for Brussels.
Though hugely popular with visitors, short-term lodgings are blamed by residents in many popular travel destinations for depriving locals of apartments for long-term rent and pushing up prices.
From New York to Tokyo and Barcelona, a growing number of cities worldwide have imposed or considered restrictions on tourist flats in recent years.
But curbs have often been followed by court challenges from rental providers and tourism operators, resulting in legal uncertainty.
The commission's Affordable Housing Act aims to provide cities with legal cover, clarifying when authorities can take action without falling foul of EU single market rules.
Cities and other relevant authorities will be allowed to limit holiday rentals as well as the purchase of property for short-term letting purposes in areas deemed "under housing stress", according to a draft seen by AFP.
The document laid out a series of parameters that needed to be met for an area to be defined as under stress, such as the ratio between house prices and incomes there.
"Population dynamics" and future housing supply and demand will also need to be taken into account, the draft said, adding any measure should be non-discriminatory, necessary and proportionate.
'Structural solutions' 
The legislation will not affect landlords that rent out their own primary residence for short periods of time.
Housing affordability has become a growing issue across the 27-nation bloc in recent years.
Property prices have surged by 60%, while rents have climbed by 20% over the past decade, leaving millions struggling to find a home they can afford, according to Brussels.
The EU says this is mainly driven by insufficient housing supply but short-term lets add extra pressure in certain areas.
Short rentals account for only about 1.2% of the European Union's housing stock but the share can reach as much as 20 percent in popular districts of some tourist destinations, according to EU data.
Holiday lets "can generate important economic and social benefits, especially for households struggling to make ends meet" but "they may also aggravate housing demand pressures in some constrained local housing markets," the EU draft read.
Yet, that's something rental providers dispute.
"For the great majority of cities, the claim that short-term rentals are driving housing stress does not survive contact with this evidence," tech lobby group CCIA wrote in a letter to the commission this month.
In some cities with restrictions, rents and hotel prices have gone up, the letter added, noting Lisbon recently overturned some of the curbs it had previously imposed.
"Europe's housing crisis needs structural solutions, and the implementation of this Act should focus on increasing the supply of homes," said an Airbnb spokesperson.

China sours on tool that helped real estate firms overhaul debt

(Sept 9): China is casting doubt on one of the key mechanisms that helped keep several major property developers including Country Garden Holdings Co out of liquidation. The China Securities Regulatory Commission has declined to accept the registration of a swathe of so-called mandatory convertible bonds, a debt-to-equity instrument that was a key part of developers’ restructuring negotiations with foreign investors, people familiar said, requesting not to be named because the matter is private. Country Garden, which has already issued a portion of the US$13 billion (RM52.91 billion) in planned offshore MCBs, was informed a few weeks ago that the securities watchdog had rejected its filing to register the instruments, according to people. Country Garden was told that it was disqualified because of its status as a discredited entity, which can result from anything from defaults to regulatory violations, the people said. Sino-Ocean Group Holding Ltd, which was exploring issuing MCBs as part of a bilateral restructuring with some private lenders, has also been informed that the CSRC would not be supportive of its registration, the people said. The rejection strikes at a little-known but increasingly important pillar of China’s property-sector debt workouts. MCBs allow distressed developers to exchange debt for securities that can later be converted into equity, helping cut repayment burdens while giving creditors a chance to benefit from any recovery. The move could undermine restructurings that have already been negotiated and limit one of the few remaining tools available to an industry that defaulted on around US$130 billion of debt. Companies don’t need to seek CSRC approval before issuing offshore MCBs. Instead, they only need to register these bonds with the regulator afterwards. The National Development and Reform Commission and State Administration of Foreign Exchange are also involved in various aspects of the approval for certain MCBs. The involvement of multiple regulators has complicated questions over which agency would be responsible if any of the MCBs instruments were to run into trouble, one person said. Representatives for the CSRC, the NDRC, SAFE and Sino-Ocean didn’t respond to requests for comment. Country Garden declined to comment. While it’s unclear whether the rejections are a procedural holdup or signal a longer halt, some property firms and financial service providers are already putting the brakes on their restructuring plans given the uncertainty, the people said. The pushback against MCBs may reflect unease among regulators that so many new shares will be created when the MCBs convert: Chinese developers’ offshore debt restructurings are ultimately set to create over 27 billion new shares through the instruments, according to estimates by Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Andrew Chan and Daniel Fan. The tools sharply dilute equity and weaken bondholder recovery, they added. More than five years since China’s property crisis began, many of the country’s developers are still in the process of restructuring their debt. Sunac China Holdings Ltd has finished a second round of debt restructuring, while CIFI Holdings Group Co is weighing a similar move, underscoring the lingering depth of the property downturn. Logan Group Co secured Hong Kong court approval in August to proceed with its restructuring scheme. Central China Real Estate Ltd and Ronshine China Holdings Ltd are among the developers still working to finalise their plans. Last month, China unveiled a slew of measures to boost financing support for homebuyers and developers. But the changes were small in isolation, stopping short of the big bang stimulus that some economists think is necessary to bring an end to the real estate slump. China’s economy showed widespread weakness in recent data, with house prices continuing to tumble. Many economists estimate that growth slipped further below the government’s annual target, sparking a call from Premier Li Qiang to ramp up supportive measures. Uploaded by Chng Shear Lane

The selection marks an important step towards turning Seoul’s headline investment pledge into actual projects and could therefore remove a persistent source of friction with Washington. In a last-minute twist, the US has asked South Korea to submit investment projects whose combined value exceeds the previously agreed US$350 billion, Yonhap reported, citing unidentified parliamentary officials. Seoul is in talks with the US to ensure its actual commitment doesn’t exceed US$350 billion, the report added. South Korea denied that part of the Yonhap report. “It is not true that the US side has requested investments exceeding US$350 billion,” South Korea’s Industry Ministry said in a statement late Tuesday. “Under the strategic investment MOU, total investment in the US will not exceed US$200 billion under any circumstances, and the annual remittance limit will not exceed US$20 billion.” It added that the scale and timing of the initial remittance have not been confirmed. Other investment proposals South Korea is considering include eight large nuclear reactors and the Alaska LNG project, Yonhap added. South Korea’s investment pledge mirrors a similar commitment by neighbouring Japan to avert higher US tariffs, though Tokyo has moved more quickly to put its US$550 billion plan into action. Japan’s first batch of projects envisages US$36 billion of investment in US oil, gas and critical-minerals projects, including a natural gas facility in Ohio. A second group calls for US$73 billion in investment in a nuclear power project spanning Tennessee and Alabama and natural gas power plants in Pennsylvania and Texas. The Industry Ministry statement said that while South Korea and the US are engaged in various discussions regarding cooperation on nuclear power plant investments, no specific details have been determined. South Korea’s parliament approved special legislation in March to implement the US investment commitment, hours after the Trump administration sought new legal grounds to impose tariffs on Seoul. My Say: Dollar dominance eroding slowly but surely

This article first appeared in Forum, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 7, 2026 - September 13, 2026 The US dollar’s role as the world’s reserve currency has been eroding gradually for decades. However, various US policies, including recent deliberately unexpected actions, have at times accelerated de-dollarisation. Dollarisation Despite warnings from economist John Maynard Keynes and others about its likely problems, Harry Dexter White, the head US delegate, imposed an indirect gold standard at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference. By fixing the gold price in dollars, the US currency became the world’s reserve currency, with other currencies pegged to it at fixed exchange rates. With this indirect gold standard, the metal’s price was fixed in US dollars. Other currencies were pegged to the dollar, strengthening its role as the dominant currency. Other arrangements that could have mitigated the problems and adverse consequences of the dollar system were effectively rejected by the US at Bretton Woods. Ninety per cent of foreign exchange market transactions now still involve the dollar. Most central bank reserves are still denominated in dollars, while the US dollar is still used to invoice around two-fifths of international trade. Just after World War II, the US economy accounted for a quarter of world output, measured in terms of purchasing power parity (PPP), and even more in nominal terms. The US share of the world economy has fallen to under 15% since. The US also accounted for a quarter of world exports at that time. Unlike most other nations, US industry was strengthened rather than destroyed during WWII. The size, liquidity and depth of US capital markets have also reinforced the dollar’s role. Its special status in the Bretton Woods dispensation conferred an “exorbitant privilege”, increasing international demand for dollar bonds. This has enabled the US government and companies to borrow at lower interest rates than others. The resulting increase in demand for dollar-denominated assets has also strengthened the greenback. Erosion of dollar dominance Since then, the US economy has become much more financialised and deindustrialised, now accounting for less than a 10th of world goods exports. However, although the US now accounts for under 15% of global income at PPP, its stock market still accounts for over three-fifths of the world’s total market capitalisation. Leading international monetary economist Barry Eichengreen’s 2022 survey of central banks’ foreign exchange reserves showed the dollar share of foreign reserves falling from 70% in 2000 to under 60% in 2021; it has since declined to below 58% in early 2025. Political economist Ben Norton suggests that the actual dollar share of foreign reserves is even lower and continues to decline. Some central banks hold other reserves off the books for fear of Western actions to freeze and seize their foreign reserves. With the US economy more deindustrialised and financialised, the dollar system has become more important in attracting foreign investors and inducing capital market bubbles from time to time. De-dollarisation accelerating De-dollarisation goes back many decades, even when the dollar-gold peg was still in place. France famously demanded gold for dollars, then shipped bullion back under armed escort. Many recent Trump administration policies have heightened international concerns about holding dollar-denominated assets. Greater Washington belligerence, including illegal tariffs, sanctions and bombings, has also accelerated de-dollarisation. President Donald Trump’s attempts to influence the US Federal Reserve and other public surveillance and regulatory institutions have also shaken public and international trust. Humiliating dismissals of allegedly recalcitrant officials have not helped. In the first half-year of Trump’s second presidential term, the dollar experienced its biggest fall since the 1973 Opec oil crisis, by over 10% against other major currencies, before fluctuating considerably. After Trump threatened massive tariffs against all other countries on April 2, 2025, fears of “a simultaneous collapse in the prices of all US assets” quickly grew. Instead of the usual flight to safety in dollar assets when crises previously loomed, it seems “The market has lost faith in US assets”, selling them down in response to new threats and uncertainties. Since then, uncertainties have worsened market and dollar volatility worldwide. Unsurprisingly, foreign governments and investors are looking for alternatives to the dollar. Eichengreen had previously expected a gradual decline in dollar dominance and a slow transition to a more balanced multi-currency reserve system. Although the US president is not the sole cause of the recent acceleration of de-dollarisation, Trump 2.0 policies have prompted monetary authorities worldwide to consider alternatives to the US dollar as the world’s reserve currency. More recently, Eichengreen has warned of a likely acceleration in the dollar’s decline, expressing concern about its adverse effects. That would threaten financial institutions holding dollar-denominated assets, causing them to lose value in foreign-currency terms. No alternative? However, Eichengreen insists “no other currency … is positioned to fill the dollar’s shoes”. Neither the euro nor the yuan has the capacity or ambition to replace the dollar. With privately issued cryptocurrencies not functioning as currencies except for mainly illicit transactions, Eichengreen expects the dollar to remain “the cleanest dirty shirt in the pile”. Jomo Kwame Sundaram is senior adviser at Khazanah Research Institute (KRI). A former economics professor, he was United Nations assistant secretary-general for economic development. He is a recipient of the Wassily Leontief Prize for Advancing the Frontiers of Economic Thought. Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy. This article first appeared in Forum, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 7, 2026 - September 13, 2026 In what US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has heralded as an Economic D-Day, the US is threatening to tighten the noose around Iran with sanctions on countries that continue to trade with it. But far from compelling others to join its efforts to isolate the Islamic Republic, the Trump administration’s mounting blunders are hastening the transition to a post-American world order. It is understandable why US “allies” are reluctant to join President Donald Trump’s costly, misbegotten war of choice. They were not consulted beforehand, and they obviously do not want to get involved now that the US has failed to topple the Iranian regime or devise a Plan B. Why, for that matter, would anyone come to help an administration that constantly berates its friends and partners, threatens to seize their territory (Greenland and Canada), and hits them with punitive tariffs? There are two ways to convince others to go along with you: persuasion and bullying. But in Trump’s case, neither is working. Aaron David Miller of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace is right to conclude that D-Day, in this case, means “desperation day”. Persuasion requires credibility. Others must believe that the administration has achievable objectives and the means to attain them. But Trump has a well-earned reputation as a liar, so no one believes anything he says. In June 2025, he claimed to have “completely and totally obliterated” Iran’s nuclear capacity, and in March he declared that the US had “literally obliterated” Iran’s military. A war that was supposed to last four weeks, or perhaps a little longer, is now into its seventh month. And everyone from the Iranians to the Canadians knows that any agreement Trump signs will be as sturdy as tissue paper. Bessent was supposed to be the cabinet member with the most credibility. But he has now squandered it with his recent, failed attempts to steer the bond and currency markets. His real motive was almost certainly to signal to his boss that he is “doing something”. But why do Trump a favour when he may turn on you the next day, as he has done to just about everyone who previously carried his water? With persuasion off the table, Trump’s only option is the one he prefers anyway: bullying and chest thumping. But this presents a problem. He and Bessent seem not to realise that the US cannot push others around as much as it once did. Nor does Trump understand the changing nature of modern war or the evolving US role in the global economy. Perpetually stuck in the past, he is unable to realise that the US’ share of global GDP (in purchasing power parity terms) has shrunk by half since the end of World War II, from roughly 30% to just under 15% in 2025. More importantly, the US has lost control of key strategic chokepoints. The advanced chips used in most cutting-edge technologies are produced in Taiwan, and China dominates magnets and rare earths production and processing. In these cases, even Trump realises that the US no longer holds all the cards. He may want to throttle the Islamic Republic’s oil revenues by targeting the buyers, but China purchases 90% of Iran’s oil exports, and it still holds a rare earths trump card. The responses to Trump’s aggression reflect these increasingly unfavourable economic realities. Seeing that American power is waning fast under Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has decided that enough is enough. He is refusing to surrender his country’s economic sovereignty to the US’ mad king — a man who cannot even prevail over Iran. The rest of the world is probably absorbing the same lesson. No one needs to tolerate such bullying. No one needs to capitulate or remain dependent on the US. A fast-changing global economic landscape offers many new opportunities for diversification. The sooner that Bessent and Trump realise how weak their hand is, the better it will be for the US and the world. If China and others resist Trump’s latest demands — as seems likely — they will neither collapse nor suffer the kinds of costs the US hopes to inflict. The economic world war Bessent has heralded would end in a stalemate, much like the impasse in the Strait of Hormuz. Once again, the US will pay a high price, and the costs it imposes on others around the world will further damage its reputation and soft power. The US used to be a role model. It stood for democracy, economic opportunity, and other values that appeal to many countries. Now, it is a model of what not to do — a cautionary tale of extreme inequality, democratic erosion, corruption and social division. The rest of the world should develop a new appreciation for the value of cooperation and the rule of law, both domestically and internationally. A world that casts off American leadership, at least for now, promises greater stability, security and prosperity for all. — Project Syndicate Joseph E Stiglitz, a Nobel laureate in economics, is a former chief economist of the World Bank, a former chair of the US President’s Council of Economic Advisers, a university professor at Columbia University, and the author, most recently, of The Road to Freedom: Economics and the Good Society (W W Norton & Company, Allen Lane, 2024) Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy.
